content.text: CCNA 200-301 STUDY MANUAL
Chapter 16
Quality of Service (QoS)

Personalised study document built from Todd Lammle, CCNA Certification Study Guide, Volume 2 (Exam 200-301, 2020), book pages 451-463. Section numbers (16.1, 16.3.1 ...) match the rows in your Notion tracker CCNA Knowledge Tracker.
| Item | Details |

| Tracker rows | Chapter 16 and sections 16.1 to 16.3.4 (9 rows, Seq 212-220). All start as Not assessed. |

| Exam versions | v1.1 (retires 2 Feb 2027): the book maps this chapter to objective 4.7, "explain the forwarding per-hop behavior (PHB) for QoS such as classification, marking, queuing, congestion, policing, shaping" (original v1.0 numbering). v2.0 (from 3 Feb 2027): QoS is not listed in Cisco's outline. See the exam table below. |

WHAT THE BOOK SAYS

Learning objective (from the book): explain how QoS treats traffic, using classification, marking, queuing, congestion management and avoidance, policing and shaping, and explain why traffic is marked at the trust boundary. This is an "explain" objective, so you need to understand the ideas and compare the tools. The book has no configuration in this chapter.

sections.title: Step 0: Pre-check (do this before you read)

content.text: Answer from memory with no looking up. Add a confidence tag: (K) I know it, (U) unsure, (G) guessing. The answer key is at the end (Answer Key A).
- Name the one-way requirements for voice traffic: latency, jitter and packet loss.
- What is the difference between a policer and a shaper? Which one delays traffic?
- Where is the trust boundary in a typical enterprise campus network?
- How many bits does DSCP use, and in which IP header field does it live?
- Name the two queuing mechanisms recommended for today's networks, and say what LLQ adds.
Mark tracker rows only when your answers are real evidence. If you were not tested on a row, leave it as Not assessed.

BOOK Quality of service (QoS) gives different priority to different kinds of traffic, applications, data flows or users, so that a certain level of performance can be guaranteed when there is contention for network resources. In simple words: when a link is busy, QoS decides whose packets go first and whose wait or get dropped.
WHY THIS MATTERS
If a link is never busy, QoS does nothing. The book says it plainly: this is not a factor on networks with excess bandwidth, but the less bandwidth you have, the more important QoS becomes.
The five problems QoS addresses (book pp. 452-453)
| Problem | What it means | Who suffers most |
| Delay | Packets meet congested lines or take a worse route, so they arrive late | Real-time apps such as voice (VoIP can fail) |
| Dropped packets | A router with full buffers drops arriving packets. TCP then retransmits, causing more delay. | Anything waiting for the missing data |
| Error | Packets are corrupted in transit and must be resent | All traffic |
| Jitter | Variation in packet delay, because packets take different paths or queue for different times | Voice and video |
| Out-of-order delivery | Packets take different paths and arrive in the wrong order, so the receiver must reassemble them | Real-time apps |
MEMORY TIP
Remember the five as Delay, Drops, Errors, Jitter, Order. QoS mainly fights delay, drops and jitter.
16.1.1 Traffic Characteristics (book pp. 453-454)
Networks carry a mix of data, voice and video. Each behaves differently, so each needs different treatment.
|  | Data | Voice | Video |
| Pattern | Smooth or bursty (unpredictable) | Smooth (steady, known arrival times) | Bursty |
| Appetite | Benign or greedy | Benign | Greedy |
| Drops | Drop insensitive | Drop sensitive | Drop sensitive |
| Delay | Delay insensitive | Delay sensitive | Delay sensitive |
| Transport | TCP retransmits lost data | UDP, needs priority | UDP, needs priority |
The book's text spells the words "insensate" and "sensate" in a few places. The correct words are insensitive and sensitive. The table above uses the correct words. UPDATED
Requirements for one-way traffic (book p. 454)
| Requirement | Voice | Video |
| Latency (delay) | � 150 ms | � 200-400 ms |
| Jitter | � 30 ms | � 30-50 ms |
| Packet loss | � 1% | � 0.1-1% |
| Bandwidth | About 128 kbps (the review question says roughly 30-128 kbps) | 384 kbps up to 20 Mbps or more |
EXAM CRITICAL
Memorise the voice numbers: 150 ms, 30 ms, 1%. The book's review question picks: smooth traffic, latency below 150 ms, bandwidth roughly 30-128 kbps.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Voice bandwidth. CHECK The book gives voice bandwidth as "only 128 kbps" in the text and "between 30 and 128 Kbps" in a review question. Real bandwidth depends on the codec and on Layer 2 overhead. Use the book's numbers for the exam and treat them as a rough guide.
Quick check 16.1
Q1. Which QoS problem is the variation in packet delay?
A. Delay
B. Jitter
C. Error
D. Out-of-order delivery
Answer: B - jitter is the variation in delay, and it hurts real-time traffic most.
Q2. Which traffic type is drop sensitive, delay sensitive and relies on UDP priority? (Choose two types.)
Answer: Voice and video - data is drop and delay insensitive and uses TCP retransmission.
Q3. What is the one-way latency limit for voice?
Answer: 150 ms or less - jitter limit 30 ms, loss limit 1%.

BOOK The trust boundary is the point in the network where packet markings are no longer automatically trusted. At that point you can create, remove or rewrite the markings. Inside the boundary, markings are accepted and acted upon.
| Term | Meaning | Examples |
| Untrusted domain | The part of the network you do not actively manage | PCs, printers, tablets |
| Trusted domain | The part with only administrator-managed devices | Switches, routers |
| Trust boundary | Where packets are classified and marked. In an enterprise campus the boundary is almost always at the edge (access) switch. | The edge switch port, or an IP phone |
WHY THIS MATTERS

Why not trust every marking? If a user's PC could mark its own traffic as top priority, it would steal bandwidth from voice. So markings arriving from the untrusted side are usually ignored, and the network re-marks the traffic itself at the boundary.
EXAM CRITICAL
The book's review question: an IP phone is a common trust boundary. PCs, printers and tablets are in the untrusted domain. The trust boundary is not always a router.
MEMORY TIP
Classify and mark as close to the source as possible, at the trust boundary. Then every device after it can simply trust the marks.
Quick check 16.2
Q4. Where is the trust boundary in a typical enterprise campus?
A. At the core router
B. At the edge (access) switch
C. At the ISP
D. At the DHCP server
Answer: B - traffic is classified and marked at the edge before entering the trusted domain.
Q5. Why are markings from an untrusted device usually ignored?
Answer: So users cannot give their own traffic unfair priority - the network re-marks the traffic itself.
BOOK QoS works as a set of tools that each do one job. The book groups them into four sets:
| Tool set | Job | Section |
| Classification and marking | Identify the traffic type and label it | 16.3.1 |
| Policing, shaping and re-marking | Limit the rate of traffic, or change its label | 16.3.2 |
| Congestion management (queuing and scheduling) | Decide which waiting packet leaves next | 16.3.3 |
| Link-specific and congestion-avoidance tools | Drop packets early in a controlled way | 16.3.4 |
MEMORY TIP
The order of treatment: Classify  Mark  Police or shape  Queue  Schedule  (Avoid congestion with WRED).
16.3.1 Classification and Marking (book pp. 455-456)

BOOK A classifier inspects a field in the packet to identify the type of traffic, so QoS knows which class it belongs to. Traffic is then sent to a policy-enforcement mechanism (marking, queuing, policing, shaping). The book warns this must not be a constant cycle, because classification costs time and resources.
Marking fields
| Marking | Layer | Size | Where it lives (book) |
| Class of Service (CoS) | 2 | 3 bits | Ethernet frame. Called the Priority Code Point (PCP) when the frame is VLAN tagged. |
| Type of Service (ToS) | 3 | 8 bits | IP header. 3 of the 8 bits are the IP precedence. |
| DSCP (DiffServ) | 3 | 6 bits | A 6-bit code point in the 8-bit DS field of the IP header. The modern replacement for IP precedence, and backwards compatible with it. |
| Class Selector (CS) | 3 | 3 bits of DSCP | Uses the same 3 bits as IP precedence, a 3-bit subset of DSCP values |
| Traffic Identifier (TID) | 2 (wireless) | 3 bits (book) | Wireless frames: 802.11 QoS control field. Like CoS, but for wireless. |
EXAM CRITICAL

Wired L2 = CoS. Wireless L2 = TID. L3 = IP precedence (old) or DSCP (new). Layer 3 markings are the most widely used because they have end-to-end significance: they survive routing. Layer 2 markings are rewritten at every hop.
The ToS byte, bit by bit
| Old ToS byte | IP precedence (3 bits) |  |  | Other ToS bits |  |  |  |  |
| New DS field | DSCP (6 bits) |  |  |  |  |  | ECN (2 bits) |  |

ADDED The book says DSCP uses 6 of the 8 bits. The remaining 2 bits are used for ECN (Explicit Congestion Notification), per RFC 3168 (Cisco's DSCP document confirms RFC 2474 had them unused and RFC 3168 defined them as ECN).
Per-hop behaviours (PHBs) you should know
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

ADDED The book does not name the PHBs, but the exam objective is literally about PHB. A per-hop behaviour is how one router treats a packet based on its DSCP value. The standard ones (checked against Cisco's DSCP document):
| PHB | DSCP (decimal) | 6-bit binary | ToS byte | Typical use |
| Default (best effort) | 0 | 000000 | 0x00 | Ordinary traffic, no special treatment |
| Class Selector CS3 | 24 | 011000 | 0x60 | Call signalling (CS values are IP precedence x 8) |
| AF11, AF21, AF31, AF41 (low drop) | 10, 18, 26, 34 | 001010, 010010, 011010, 100010 | 0x28, 0x48, 0x68, 0x88 | Assured forwarding classes. AF41 is commonly used for interactive video. |
| EF (Expedited Forwarding) | 46 | 101110 | 0xB8 | Voice. Low loss, low latency, low jitter, assured bandwidth. Gets strict priority. |
MEMORY TIP

AF naming: AFxy: x is the class (1-4, higher = better) and y is the drop precedence (1 = lowest drop chance, 3 = highest). DSCP = 8 x x + 2 x y, so AF41 = 8x4 + 2x1 = 34. EF is just 46. Class selectors are multiples of 8 (CS1 = 8, CS3 = 24, CS5 = 40).
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Which values for which traffic? CHECK Voice = EF (46), interactive video = AF41 (34) and call signalling = CS3 (24) are the common Cisco recommendations. These are guidelines, and your organisation may differ. The three values are listed in Cisco's DSCP document, but the "which traffic goes where" mapping is general practice that I did not verify against a Cisco design guide.
Three ways to classify traffic (book p. 456)
| Method | How it works | Cost |
| Markings | Looks at existing Layer 2 or Layer 3 markings (CoS, DSCP) and classifies by them | Cheap |
| Addressing | Looks at header fields: source and destination interface, Layer 2 and 3 addresses, Layer 4 port numbers. Groups traffic by device (IP) and by type (port). | Cheap |
| Application signatures | Looks inside the payload (deep packet inspection) | Most CPU intensive |
NBAR (Network Based Application Recognition)

BOOK NBAR is a classifier that does deep-packet inspection on Layers 4 to 7. It is needed because you cannot always identify an application from Layer 3 and 4 alone. NBAR compares the payload with a signature database called a Packet Description Language Module (PDLM). It is the most CPU-intensive technique compared with addresses, ports or ACLs.
| NBAR mode | What it does |
| Passive | Gives real-time statistics: applications by protocol or interface, bit rate, packet and byte counts |
| Active | Classifies applications so that marking can be applied and QoS policies can act on them |
Quick check 16.3.1
Q6. Which is a Layer 2 QoS marking?
A. DSCP
B. IP precedence
C. CoS
D. ToS
Answer: C - CoS is a 3-bit Layer 2 marking (PCP in a VLAN tag). DSCP, IP precedence and ToS are Layer 3.
Q7. How many bits are in DSCP, and in which header?
Answer: 6 bits, inside the 8-bit DS field of the IP header - the other 2 bits are ECN.
Q8. Which advanced tool classifies applications by looking deep into the payload?
A. NBAR
B. ACL
C. CoS
D. WRED
Answer: A - NBAR does Layer 4-7 deep-packet inspection.
Q9. What DSCP value is EF, and what traffic normally uses it?
Answer: 46; voice - EF gives low loss, low latency, low jitter.
16.3.2 Policing, Shaping, and Re-marking (book pp. 456-457)

BOOK Once traffic is identified and marked, you act on it. If traffic exceeds the allowed bandwidth it can be delayed, dropped or re-marked to avoid congestion. Policers and shapers are the two tools that identify and respond to traffic problems, and both are rate-limiters.
|  | Policer | Shaper |
| What it does to excess traffic | Drops it (or re-marks it to a lower class) | Delays it in a queue until it can be sent |
| Delay and jitter | None added | Adds delay and jitter |
| TCP resends | Causes many TCP resends (higher drop probability) | Fewer TCP resends |

| Where deployed | Ingress preferably (drop early what will be dropped anyway). Can also be used on egress. | Usually egress, between the enterprise and the ISP, to stay within the contracted rate (the SLA) |
| Reaction | Instant decision | Smooths the traffic |
MEMORY TIP
Policers drop. Shapers delay. Shapers add delay and jitter but few resends. Policers add no delay but cause more resends.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

A tiny numbers example. ADDED Offered traffic is 10 Mbps for one second and the contract rate is 4 Mbps. A policer sends 4 Mbps and drops the other 6 (or re-marks it). A shaper also sends 4 Mbps, but queues the extra 6 and sends it in the next moments at the 4 Mbps rate (about 1.5 more seconds). Nothing is lost if the queue is big enough, but everything is delayed. (Simplified: real devices also allow a small burst.) CHECK
WHY THIS MATTERS

Why shape toward the ISP? If you send more than your contracted rate, the provider will police you and drop the excess. By shaping first, you decide what waits instead of letting the provider drop traffic at random.
Re-marking

Re-marking means changing a packet's existing marking, for example setting DSCP to a lower value when a policer decides the traffic is over its rate. The book lists it in the same group as policing and shaping.
Quick check 16.3.2
Q10. Which QoS mechanism drops traffic if a session uses more than its allotted bandwidth?
A. Congestion management
B. Shaping
C. Policing
D. Marking
Answer: C - policing drops (or re-marks) excess traffic. Shaping delays it.
Q11. Which mechanism adds delay and jitter but causes fewer TCP resends?
Answer: Shaping - queued packets are delayed, not dropped.
Q12. Where is a shaper usually deployed?
Answer: On the egress side toward the ISP - to stay within the contract rate (SLA).
16.3.3 Tools for Managing Congestion (book pp. 457-460)

BOOK When traffic exceeds network resources, packets wait in queues (temporary storage). Queuing avoids dropping packets that cannot be sent immediately. The book makes a surprising point: traffic like VoIP is often better off being dropped at once than queued, unless you can guarantee enough delay-free bandwidth for it.
Queuing and scheduling are two separate jobs
| Job | What it does | When it runs |
| Queuing (buffering) | Orders packets in the output buffers. When queues fill, higher-priority packets can be sent before lower-priority ones. | Only when there is congestion |
| Scheduling | Decides which packet is sent out next | Always, whether or not the link is congested |
Three scheduling mechanisms
| Mechanism | How it works | Good | Bad |
| Strict priority | Low-priority queues are served only when high-priority queues are empty | Great for the high-priority traffic | Low-priority queues can starve (never get served) |
| Round-robin | Queues are served in a fixed sequence, one after the other | No starvation, looks fair | Real-time traffic suffers badly |
| Weighted fair | Queues are weighted, so some are served more often than others | No starvation, and real-time traffic can get priority | No guarantee of exact bandwidth |

BOOK Queuing is mostly a Layer 3 process, but it can also occur at Layer 2 or Layer 1. The Layer 1 queue is the transmit ring (TX-ring). If the TX-ring fills, packets are pushed back to the Layer 2 and 3 queues. That is when QoS becomes active on the device.
Legacy queuing methods (book p. 459)
| Method | What it is | Problem |
| FIFO (First In First Out) | A single queue. Packets leave in arrival order. | No priority at all |
| PQ (Priority Queuing) | Four queues. Lower queues served only when higher queues are empty. | Low-priority traffic may never be sent |
| CQ (Custom Queuing) | Up to 16 queues, round-robin. Prevents starvation and gives traffic guarantees. | No strict priority for real-time traffic, so VoIP can still be dropped |
| WFQ (Weighted Fair Queuing) | Divides bandwidth by the number of flows. The book calls it Cisco's default. | No guarantee for a particular flow |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Default queuing. CHECK The book calls WFQ "the Cisco default". As far as I know, the default depends on the interface speed (WFQ on slow serial interfaces, FIFO on fast interfaces). I did not verify this in this session, so for the exam use the book's statement.
The two modern methods: CBWFQ and LLQ (book pp. 459-460)
|  | CBWFQ (Class-Based Weighted Fair Queuing) | LLQ (Low Latency Queuing) |
| What it gives | Fairness and bandwidth guarantees for all traffic classes | CBWFQ plus a strict-priority queue for real-time traffic |
| Latency guarantee | No | Yes, for the priority queue |
| Best for | Data traffic management | Data and real-time traffic (voice and video) |
MEMORY TIP
LLQ = CBWFQ + one priority queue. Take the priority queue away from LLQ and you are left with CBWFQ, which the book says is only used for data-traffic networks.
EXAM CRITICAL
Exam Essentials: the two queuing mechanisms you should use today are CBWFQ and LLQ. Know the starvation problem with strict priority and why round-robin hurts real-time traffic.
Quick check 16.3.3
Q13. What is queue starvation, and which scheduling method can cause it?
Answer: Low-priority queues never get served; strict priority scheduling - strict priority only serves lower queues when higher queues are empty.
Q14. Which queuing mechanism provides both bandwidth and latency guarantees for voice and data?
A. FIFO
B. WFQ
C. CBWFQ
D. LLQ
Answer: D - LLQ adds a strict-priority queue to CBWFQ.
Q15. Does scheduling happen only during congestion?
Answer: No. Queuing is activated by congestion; scheduling always runs - scheduling decides the next packet out of the interface.
16.3.4 Tools for Congestion Avoidance (book pp. 460-461)
BOOK TCP's sliding windows give flow control. When loss occurs TCP cuts its sending rate sharply, then speeds up again once things clear. That behaviour causes problems on busy links:
| Term | Meaning |
| Tail drop | Dropping packets as they arrive because the queue is full. It wastes bandwidth, because TCP just resends the data. |
| TCP global synchronization | When many senders all lose packets at the same time, they all slow down together, then all speed up together, in waves. Much of the bandwidth sits unused. |
| Congestion avoidance | Starts dropping some packets before the queue fills, using weights instead of pure randomness. |

| WRED (Weighted Random Early Detection) | Cisco's method: drops packets early, with higher-precedence traffic getting lower loss rates. This protects important traffic such as VoIP over less important traffic. |
MEMORY TIP
Queuing manages the front of the queue (which packet leaves next). Congestion avoidance manages the back (which packets are dropped when it is filling up).
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

ADDED WRED uses the DSCP or IP precedence marking to decide how aggressively to drop. That is why marking comes first in the QoS order. In the AF classes, a higher drop precedence (AF13, for example) is dropped earlier than a lower one (AF11).
Quick check 16.3.4
Q16. Which of these is a congestion-avoidance mechanism?
A. LMI
B. WRED
C. QPM
D. NBAR
Answer: B - WRED drops packets early, weighted by priority.
Q17. What is TCP global synchronization?
Answer: Many TCP senders slow down and speed up together after loss, so bandwidth is used in waves and partly wasted - WRED avoids it by dropping packets early at different times.

sections.title: A Look at How QoS Is Configured (MQC)

content.text: ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

ADDED Not in the book and not required for the "explain" objective. The book has no QoS configuration, but seeing the commands makes the ideas concrete. Cisco configures QoS with the Modular QoS CLI (MQC) in three steps. This sample is standard MQC; I did not run it. CHECK
Illustrative MQC policy: voice gets a strict-priority LLQ queue CHECK
! 1. CLASSIFY: class-map says which traffic
Router(config)# class-map match-any VOICE
Router(config-cmap)# match dscp ef
Router(config-cmap)# exit
! 2. TREAT: policy-map says what to do with each class
Router(config)# policy-map WAN-OUT
Router(config-pmap)# class VOICE
Router(config-pmap-c)# priority percent 20
Router(config-pmap-c)# exit
Router(config-pmap)# class class-default
Router(config-pmap-c)# fair-queue
Router(config-pmap-c)# exit
Router(config-pmap)# exit
! 3. APPLY: service-policy attaches it to an interface
Router(config)# interface gigabitEthernet 0/1
Router(config-if)# service-policy output WAN-OUT
Router(config-if)# end
Router# show policy-map interface gigabitEthernet 0/1
- class-map match-any VOICE creates a class named VOICE. match dscp ef puts any packet marked EF (46) into it. This is classification.
- policy-map WAN-OUT creates a policy. class VOICE then priority percent 20 gives voice a strict-priority queue limited to 20 percent of the bandwidth. That is the LLQ part.
- class class-default is the catch-all for everything else. fair-queue shares what is left fairly. (Using bandwidth percent instead would make it a CBWFQ class with a guaranteed share.)
- service-policy output WAN-OUT applies the policy to traffic leaving the interface. show policy-map interface shows the counters for each class.
Two other MQC actions to recognise: police (policing) and shape average (shaping). CHECK Exact options vary by platform, so check ? on your device.

sections.title: Which QoS Tool Solves Which Problem?

content.text: ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)
ADDED Exam questions often give a symptom and ask for the tool. This table is the quick map.
| Symptom | Best tool | Why |
| Voice is choppy on a busy WAN link | LLQ (strict-priority queue) with voice marked EF | Gives voice low latency and guaranteed bandwidth |
| The ISP is dropping traffic that exceeds the contracted rate | Shaping on the egress toward the ISP | You delay the excess yourself and stay within the SLA |
| Users set their own traffic to the highest priority | Trust boundary: ignore and re-mark at the edge switch | Untrusted markings must not decide priority |
| A bulk transfer is hogging a link | Policing it (or give it a limited CBWFQ share) | Limits the rate of that class |
| Several TCP flows slow down and speed up in waves | WRED (congestion avoidance) | Early weighted drops break the synchronization |
| Low-priority queues never get any bandwidth | Change from strict priority to a weighted method (CBWFQ), or limit the priority queue | Strict priority can starve other queues |
| You must find out which applications are on the network | NBAR (passive mode) | Deep-packet inspection statistics |
| Traffic must be recognised by application, not port | NBAR (active mode) for classification and marking | Application signatures |
CHECK These mappings follow the chapter's concepts and standard QoS practice. They were not tested on equipment.
| Topic | Remember |
| Why QoS | Gives different traffic different priority when a link is congested. Fights delay, drops, errors, jitter and out-of-order delivery. |
| Traffic types | Data: insensitive, TCP retransmits. Voice: smooth, drop and delay sensitive, UDP, �150 ms, �30 ms jitter, �1% loss. Video: bursty, greedy, drop and delay sensitive. |
| Trust boundary | Where markings stop being trusted and traffic is classified and marked. Usually the edge switch or an IP phone. Untrusted = PCs, printers. |
| Marking | CoS 3 bits (L2 wired, PCP). TID (L2 wireless). IP precedence 3 bits of ToS. DSCP 6 bits of the DS field (+2 ECN). L3 marking is end-to-end. |
| PHBs | Default 0, CS3 24, AF41 34, EF 46 (voice). DSCP = 8x+2y for AFxy. ToS byte = DSCP x 4. |
| Classification | By markings, addressing (IP, ports) or application signatures (NBAR, most CPU). NBAR: passive (statistics) or active (classify for marking). |
| Policer vs shaper | Both rate-limiters. Policer drops or re-marks, no delay, more TCP resends, ingress. Shaper delays, adds jitter, fewer resends, egress toward ISP. |
| Queuing vs scheduling | Queuing only during congestion. Scheduling always. Strict priority can starve; round-robin hurts real-time; weighted fair is the better compromise. |
| Legacy queues | FIFO, PQ (4 queues), CQ (16 queues), WFQ (by flow). |
| Modern queues | CBWFQ (bandwidth guarantees, data) and LLQ (CBWFQ + strict-priority queue, latency guarantee, voice). |
| Congestion avoidance | Tail drop wastes bandwidth. TCP global synchronization wastes bandwidth. WRED drops early, weighted by priority. |
| MQC | class-map (classify)  policy-map (treat)  service-policy (apply). |

Status choices: Not assessed � Know � Partially understand � Need to learn � Needs revision.
- Latency � 150 ms, jitter � 30 ms, packet loss � 1% (one way).
- Both are rate-limiters. A policer drops (or re-marks) excess traffic and adds no delay. A shaper delays excess traffic in a queue, adding delay and jitter but causing fewer TCP resends.
- At the edge (access) switch, or at an IP phone. Traffic is classified and marked there.
- 6 bits, in the 8-bit DS field of the IP header (the old ToS byte). The other 2 bits are ECN.
- CBWFQ and LLQ. LLQ adds a strict-priority queue for real-time traffic, which gives a latency guarantee as well as bandwidth.

sections.title: How far this has been tested

content.text: Nothing in this document was run on real Cisco hardware. Commands and lab results are written from standard usage. Test them and correct anything that differs on your platform.
For each situation, name the mechanism: classification, marking, policing, shaping, congestion management (queuing/scheduling) or congestion avoidance. Write answers first.
| # | Situation |
| 1 | A router checks the DSCP value and decides a packet is voice. |
| 2 | An edge switch overwrites the CoS value that a user's PC sent. |
| 3 | Traffic over 50 Mbps is thrown away at the ingress of the WAN router. |
| 4 | Traffic over 50 Mbps is held in a buffer and sent more slowly. |
| 5 | Voice packets are always sent before data packets when the output queue is busy. |
| 6 | The router starts dropping low-precedence packets before the queue is full. |
| 7 | NBAR inspects the payload to identify the application. |
**What the book says**

Solutions. 1. Classification. 2. Marking (re-marking at the trust boundary). 3. Policing. 4. Shaping. 5. Congestion management (queuing and scheduling, LLQ). 6. Congestion avoidance (WRED). 7. Classification (application signatures).

labs.title: Decode DSCP and the ToS byte (paper, 15 minutes)

content.text: Convert each DSCP value to its 6-bit binary and to the 8-bit ToS byte (the DSCP bits followed by two zero ECN bits). Then name the PHB. Do not use a calculator for the first three.
| # | DSCP (decimal) | 6-bit binary | ToS byte (hex) | PHB |
**What the book says**

Solutions (checked by script). 1. 46 = 101110, ToS byte 10111000 = 0xB8, EF. 2. 34 = 100010, ToS byte 0x88, AF41. 3. 24 = 011000, ToS byte 0x60, CS3 (IP precedence 3). 4. 0 = 000000, ToS byte 0x00, Default (best effort). 5. 26 = 011010, ToS byte 0x68, AF31.
Method: the ToS byte is the DSCP value times 4 (shift left two bits). 46 x 4 = 184 = 0xB8.

A branch has a 10 Mbps WAN link from a provider that polices traffic above 10 Mbps on its side. Applications on the branch LAN can burst to 100 Mbps. Answer: (a) Which tool do you put on your router's WAN egress and why? (b) What side effect will you see on voice if you use it without a priority queue? (c) What would happen to TCP traffic if you let the provider's policer do the limiting instead?
**What the book says**

Solutions. (a) Shaping at about 10 Mbps, so your router delays the excess itself instead of the provider dropping it. (b) Shaping adds delay and jitter to everything held in the queue, including voice, so give voice a priority queue (LLQ). (c) The provider's policer would drop the excess, causing many TCP resends and lower throughput.

Draw a small campus: PCs and a printer on an access switch, an IP phone with a PC plugged into it, a distribution switch, a core switch and a router to the ISP. Mark: (1) the untrusted and trusted domains, (2) where classification and marking should happen, (3) which markings you would accept and which you would ignore.
**What the book says**

Expected answer. The boundary is at the access switch (and the IP phone if it is trusted). PCs and the printer are untrusted, and their markings are ignored or re-marked. After the boundary, distribution, core and the WAN router trust the markings. Mark as close to the source as possible.

labs.title: Optional MQC lab (Packet Tracer or real device, 25 minutes)

content.text: - Use two routers and two PCs. Configure the policy from the MQC section on the router interface that leads to the slower link.
- Run show policy-map and show policy-map interface <interface>.
- Ping across the link and run show policy-map interface again. Look at the packet counters for each class.

Expected result: the class counters change as matching traffic passes. Pings are not marked EF, so they should land in class-default. CHECK Packet Tracer's QoS support may be limited or missing for some commands, so if a command is rejected, write down which one. This lab is optional because the exam objective is to explain QoS, not to configure it.

content.text: Q1 Which QoS problem is the variation in packet delay?
A. Delay
B. Jitter
C. Error
D. Out-of-order delivery
Answer: B - jitter is the variation in delay, and it hurts real-time traffic most.
Q2 Which traffic type is drop sensitive, delay sensitive and relies on UDP priority? (Choose two types.)
Answer: Voice and video - data is drop and delay insensitive and uses TCP retransmission.
Q3 What is the one-way latency limit for voice?
Answer: 150 ms or less - jitter limit 30 ms, loss limit 1%.
Q4 Where is the trust boundary in a typical enterprise campus?
A. At the core router
B. At the edge (access) switch
C. At the ISP
D. At the DHCP server
Answer: B - traffic is classified and marked at the edge before entering the trusted domain.
Q5 Why are markings from an untrusted device usually ignored?
Answer: So users cannot give their own traffic unfair priority - the network re-marks the traffic itself.
Q6 Which is a Layer 2 QoS marking?
A. DSCP
B. IP precedence
C. CoS
D. ToS
Answer: C - CoS is a 3-bit Layer 2 marking (PCP in a VLAN tag). DSCP, IP precedence and ToS are Layer 3.
Q7 How many bits are in DSCP, and in which header?
Answer: 6 bits, inside the 8-bit DS field of the IP header - the other 2 bits are ECN.
Q8 Which advanced tool classifies applications by looking deep into the payload?
A. NBAR
B. ACL
C. CoS
D. WRED
Answer: A - NBAR does Layer 4-7 deep-packet inspection.
Q9 What DSCP value is EF, and what traffic normally uses it?
Answer: 46; voice - EF gives low loss, low latency, low jitter.
Q10 Which QoS mechanism drops traffic if a session uses more than its allotted bandwidth?
A. Congestion management
B. Shaping
C. Policing
D. Marking
Answer: C - policing drops (or re-marks) excess traffic. Shaping delays it.
Q11 Which mechanism adds delay and jitter but causes fewer TCP resends?
Answer: Shaping - queued packets are delayed, not dropped.
Q12 Where is a shaper usually deployed?
Answer: On the egress side toward the ISP - to stay within the contract rate (SLA).
Q13 What is queue starvation, and which scheduling method can cause it?
Answer: Low-priority queues never get served; strict priority scheduling - strict priority only serves lower queues when higher queues are empty.
Q14 Which queuing mechanism provides both bandwidth and latency guarantees for voice and data?
A. FIFO
B. WFQ
C. CBWFQ
D. LLQ
Answer: D - LLQ adds a strict-priority queue to CBWFQ.
Q15 Does scheduling happen only during congestion?
Answer: No. Queuing is activated by congestion; scheduling always runs - scheduling decides the next packet out of the interface.
Q16 Which of these is a congestion-avoidance mechanism?
A. LMI
B. WRED
C. QPM
D. NBAR
Answer: B - WRED drops packets early, weighted by priority.
Q17 What is TCP global synchronization?
Answer: Many TCP senders slow down and speed up together after loss, so bandwidth is used in waves and partly wasted - WRED avoids it by dropping packets early at different times.
Q18 A user complains that voice calls break up only during large file transfers. Which change best helps?
A. Use FIFO queuing
B. Add an LLQ priority queue for voice marked EF
C. Disable QoS
D. Use a policer on voice
Answer: B - LLQ gives voice a strict-priority queue with low latency.
Q19 Which statement is true? (Choose one.)
A. Policers delay traffic, shapers drop it
B. Shapers delay traffic, policers drop or re-mark it
C. Both always delay traffic
D. Neither is a rate-limiter
Answer: B - both are rate-limiters. Shapers delay, policers drop or re-mark.
Q20 How many bits does the DSCP value use, and how many of the DS field's bits are left for ECN?
Answer: 6 bits; 2 bits - 6 + 2 = 8 bits in the DS field.
Q21 Which two of these are Layer 3 QoS markings? CoS, DSCP, IP precedence, TID
Answer: D - SCP and IP precedence - CoS is wired Layer 2; TID is wireless Layer 2.
Q22 Which DSCP value does voice normally use, and what is its PHB name?
Answer: 46, EF (Expedited Forwarding) - EF gives strict priority with low loss, delay and jitter.
Q23 Name the problem when low-priority queues never get any bandwidth.
Answer: Starvation (caused by strict priority scheduling) - weighted methods avoid it.
Q24 Which QoS tool introduces jitter and delay but results in fewer TCP resends?
Answer: Shaping - it queues excess traffic instead of dropping it.
Q25 What is the difference between queuing and scheduling?
Answer: Queuing holds packets when the interface is congested; scheduling chooses which packet leaves next, always - queuing is activated by congestion, scheduling is not.
Q26 At what point in the network should traffic be marked, and why?
Answer: A - t the trust boundary (usually the edge switch), as close to the source as possible - so every later device can trust the marking.
Q27 What does LLQ add to CBWFQ?
Answer: A - strict-priority queue for real-time traffic, giving a latency guarantee - without it, CBWFQ is only suited to data.
Q28 Which IP precedence value matches CS3, and what is the ToS byte for DSCP 24?
Answer: Precedence 3; 0x60 - 24 = 011000, shifted left two bits = 01100000.
Q29 Which tool keeps important traffic from being dropped first when a queue starts to fill?
Answer: WRED - it drops lower-precedence traffic earlier.
Q30 In which direction (ingress or egress) is a policer usually placed, and why?
Answer: Ingress, because traffic that will be dropped anyway should be dropped as early as possible - shapers are usually placed on egress.
